19 A truck of mass 500 kg moves from rest at the top of a section of track 400 m long and 30 m high,
as shown. The frictional force acting on the truck is 250 N throughout its journey.
400 m
30 m
What is the final speed of the truck?
A
14 m s–1
B
24 m s–1
C
31 m s–1
D
190 m s–1

hints: Notice the two different distances: $30 \text{ m}$ is the vertical height for gravitational potential energy and $400 \text{ m}$ is the slope distance for friction.
Connect energy loss to work done: initial $mgh$ is shared between work against the $250 \text{ N}$ friction force and final kinetic energy.
Calculate $mgh - Fd = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ with $m = 500 \text{ kg}$, then rearrange to $v = \sqrt{2 \times \text{remaining energy}/m}$.
walkthrough: Start from rest, so initial kinetic energy is zero and initial gravitational potential energy is $E_p = mgh$ with $m = 500 \text{ kg}$ and $h = 30 \text{ m}$.
Use $E_p = 500 \times 9.81 \times 30 = 147150 \text{ J}$, about $147 \text{ kJ}$ available from the descent.
Work done against constant friction is $W = Fd$ with $F = 250 \text{ N}$ along the $d = 400 \text{ m}$ slope, so $W = 250 \times 400 = 100000 \text{ J}$.
Apply conservation with loss: final $E_k = E_p - W = 147150 - 100000 = 47150 \text{ J}$.
Rounded to two significant figures this is about $14 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. This is option A.

A.explanation: Final kinetic energy is initial $mgh$ minus work done against friction, giving $v$ about $14 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: This is close to ignoring the $100000 \text{ J}$ of work done by the $250 \text{ N}$ friction force over $400 \text{ m}$.

C.explanation: This uses $400 \text{ m}$ as the vertical drop in $mgh$ instead of the $30 \text{ m}$ height.

D.explanation: This mistakes the remaining energy in $\text{J}$ for speed and omits the $v = \sqrt{2KE/m}$ square-root step.
